tagline: A two-lane border road through the Sonoran Desert’s cactus country
intro: South of Why, State Route 85 crosses Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument on two lanes before reaching the Mexican border at Lukeville. The monument’s landscape includes volcanic mountains, washes and broad valleys. Arizona designated a 21-mile segment as the Organ Pipe Cactus Parkway in 2008; ADOT identifies the desert vegetation and scenery as the reasons for that recognition. The monument is also an International Biosphere Reserve. Human life in this Sonoran Desert landscape extends back thousands of years, alongside its communities of plants and animals.

The larger highway corridor developed in connection with Ajo’s copper industry. Maricopa and Pima counties graded the road from Gila Bend to the junction that became Why, and SR 85 entered the state highway system in 1936. After the monument’s establishment in 1937, paving reached from Why to Lukeville in 1942 and 1943. That southern road became part of SR 85 in 1955.

Begin at Why’s junction with SR 86 and follow SR 85 south into the monument. At the Kris Eggle Visitor Center, a short nature trail introduces desert plants and rare Quitobaquito pupfish. Lukeville marks the highway’s southern end; beyond the border, the road continues into Sonoyta as Mexican Federal Highway 8.

moments.title: Why
moments.text: Why’s name outlasted the road junction that supplied it. State Routes 85 and 86 once met in a Y shape here; ADOT later replaced that junction with a conventional intersection farther south for traffic safety. The community lies north of Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, near the western edge of the Tohono Oʼodham Indian Reservation. The junction divides three onward routes: SR 86 runs east toward Tucson, SR 85 northwest toward Ajo, and SR 85 south through the monument to Lukeville. Why lies ten miles south of Ajo, at this junction of the two state highways.

moments.title: Kris Eggle Visitor Center
moments.text: The visitor center’s tenth-mile nature trail includes rare Quitobaquito pupfish alongside cacti and other desert plants. An exhibit room introduces the monument, which was set aside in 1937 as an example of the Sonoran Desert. The organ pipe cactus has several upright stems rising from a short trunk near ground level. It grows predominantly on rocky hillsides and is sensitive to frost, making it rarer in low desert areas where frost is more frequent. The cactus’s English name comes from its resemblance to a pipe organ; its stems seldom branch, instead extending from their tips.

moments.title: Lukeville
moments.text: Lukeville is a border town entirely within Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument. Charles Luke, brother of World War I aviator Frank Luke, started the community. An executive order established its port of entry in 1949, primarily for passenger vehicles and pedestrians. The road connects Arizona’s SR 85 with Mexican Federal Highway 8 in Sonoyta. In 2011, modifications funded by the Federal Highway Administration and Mexican businesses provided for truck inspections and improved traffic flow. Much of the crossing’s traffic heads for the beach town of Puerto Peñasco in Sonora, linking the desert highway to a destination beyond the border.
